He wakes with a headache and a strange flatness, and there is nobody in his head who was not there two years ago. The clock says he has lost more than sleep. He gets up, showers, walks to the platform for work, and gets on the other train instead. He could not tell you why.

Two years earlier, at the end of that same line, a man with nothing to say to anyone ended up talking to a woman with dyed hair on a beach full of strangers. They broke the window of a shuttered house on the shore and slept on the boards, and in the morning neither of them had anywhere else to be.

He walks out onto frozen sand and finds a woman with dyed hair already standing on it, as though she had been waiting, though she couldn't have been.

Two years earlier again, small rooms, cold weather: the ice of the frozen river, steam on the windows of a noodle house, the drive-in with the sound turned down. He was happy in a way he could not describe to anyone. She had found somewhere she could stop moving.

They drive back into the city talking too easily for strangers. Outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time, not the first.

Before that: the same rooms turned against them. She drank and he counted it; he said nothing and she called it contempt. Each of them had learned exactly which sentence did the most damage.

Upstairs, she puts the kettle on and looks at him like she's deciding something, and he cannot say why he feels he already knows this kitchen.

Before that: she came in at two in the morning having put his car into something on the way, and the fight that started over the dent finished somewhere neither of them could come back from. She took a bag and went.

At a clinic in a shabby office building she paid to have a man taken out of her head. He went to make it up with her at the bookshop and she looked at him like a customer; there was a young man behind the counter, Peck, and she was laughing at everything he said.

Two friends handed Tobias the form letter the clinic had sent to everyone she knew, and he took it straight to the director, Dr. Hallam, and asked for the same thing done to him.

He filled two carrier bags with everything that had her in it, so the machine could find what it was pinned to. That night Dell and Peck let themselves into his flat, put the cap on him while he slept, and worked through the map room by room. Peck put the bagged keepsakes into his own coat.

Inside his own head Tobias stood in the worst of it and watched the rooms lose their walls while he was still in them. When the machine reached the ones he wanted to keep, he ran, carrying her into places she had never been — a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map didn't go.

Outside, Dell and Rosa were drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear when the map stopped meaning anything, and nobody noticed for a long time. Dr. Hallam was called out at three to put it back on the rails; Rosa kissed him in the hallway, and his wife, arriving behind him, told her exactly why she'd always felt that way about him, and that it had been taken out of her once already.

The last thing left was the shore house, the night they met. In the doorway of a room that was already going, Ivy told him to walk out — and then to come and find her at the coast.

Now, in her flat, two envelopes arrive on the same morning: Rosa, quitting, has mailed every patient their own file, the tapes, the reasons they gave. They sit in the stairwell and listen to their own voices tearing each other apart. Ivy runs down two flights, stands on the pavement a long time, and comes back up.

They decide to do it anyway.

There is a heart in Aaron's chest that used to belong to somebody else, and he cannot stop counting its beats, the way he used to count staircases and how many he could climb before the breath went out of him. He hired a man in a car park to tell him whose it was, and the man said this is against every rule there is, and took the money anyway.

Lena keeps the girls' drawings on the wall behind the kitchen table where she does the cocaine now, methodically, the way she once kept a garden. She used to be somebody else. There was a husband who adored her and a fixed rate on a house and two small girls doing the school run, and then there was a corridor and a side room and a doctor telling her about all three of them while she was still absorbing the first sentence.

Wes crosses the country cleaning motel rooms, having put down, on the same day, his wife and his God. Before that there was a certainty in him that his wife watched like weather coming, a boys' baseball team on Saturdays, scripture on both forearms. Before that there was a pickup at a crossing, the engine still running while it sat a hundred yards on, the small backward roll of it, and then the going.

Aaron followed Lena to a swimming pool for a week until being in the water at her hour stopped being a coincidence, and within a fortnight he was in her house, not telling her the thing that mattered. He told his wife Della he wasn't coming back, and did not want the child she was trying to conceive from what was left in the freezer — the same freezer she'd asked him to sign for across a kitchen table, in the last weeks when a doctor had told him his heart was finished and the only thing that would help was somebody else dying at the right time. Della said the true thing: that he was spending a life somebody else had paid for.

He said it to Lena badly, in her own kitchen — what was beating in his chest — and she threw him out that night with everything he'd brought, and four days later took him back knowing exactly what he was carrying.

Somewhere behind all of it a chest had been opened in an operating theatre and a heart put into it that had been beating an hour before in somebody else, and a man had woken able to breathe for the first time in months. Somewhere behind that a man had walked into a police station on his own and told a desk sergeant what he'd done at a crossing and how far he'd driven afterward, and was back inside within the month.

Lena said she could not keep breathing in the same country as the man who did it, until it was the only thing left in the house, and Aaron bought a pistol from a man in a lock-up. Wes, released early on somebody's recommendation, had already looked at his own gate, at Nita and the family waiting for him there, and kept walking, four hundred miles to a motel where none of it could follow him.

It followed him anyway. Aaron got him against a wall in the dark and could not make his hand finish it; the shot went somewhere that wouldn't kill, and he stood over him telling him to run. Instead Wes came to their door bleeding through his shirt and asked to be finished, and Aaron turned the gun around and put it into his own chest.

They got him into a car with the horn down, and on the table the borrowed heart stopped anyway, the one that had started at a crossing and gone into another man's body only to be spent on this. Wes went home, finally, to the wife and the God he'd left at a gate. Lena went home alone, carrying, though she didn't yet know how to say it, the last thing anyone had asked her to keep.

THE WATCH

The boy's father had died in a camp somewhere with the watch pressed under a floorboard for two years, and when the veteran came home he did not go to see his own family first. He went to a small front room, sat the boy down, and put the gold watch in his hands and said nothing else needed to be said. Denny was nine. He wore it under his sleeve for the rest of his life the way other men wear a scar.

He had it on him the night he took a dive money in a near-empty bar from a man called Otis, and he had it on him the night he decided, in the ring, under lights, that he was not going to fall in the fifth after all. He put the other man down for good and was gone through a side door before the crowd worked out what it had watched.

Weeks later, in a motel on the edge of town, he asked Marielle if she'd packed it. She hadn't. It was sitting on the bedside table in a flat that Otis's men would already be watching, and Denny understood that the one thing he could not leave behind was the one thing he could not go back for. He went back anyway. He let himself in, found it exactly where it had been left, and was standing at the counter fastening it to his wrist when a hitman named Rollo came out of the bathroom and discovered the submachine gun on the counter was nearer to Denny's hand than his own gun was to his.

The watch was on Denny's wrist in the pawnshop basement too, ticking against the ropes while Otis, who he'd nearly killed with a car an hour before, knelt a few feet away getting the worse of it from the men who'd dragged them both down there. Denny had his hands free and was at the door. He stopped, took a sword down off the wall instead, and went back for a man who'd been hunting him. Otis, after, called them square, on the condition Denny never showed his face in the city again.

He collected Marielle from the motel, put her on the back of a motorcycle lifted from the pawnshop, and rode out with the watch still on his wrist, ticking the same as it had in the camp, in the front room, in the ring.

Long before any of that, Rollo and Marcus had crossed the whole city arguing about what a hamburger was called abroad, and stood in a corridor debating whether a foot massage was worth a man's life, before going in and shooting a young man named Tobin over Marcus's recited scripture and a briefcase Otis wanted back. A fourth man came out of a bathroom in that same flat and put a full revolver's worth of rounds into the air around them without touching either one, and Marcus decided, standing in the pattern of holes behind him, that he'd been given a warning. In the car after, Rollo's gun went off on its own and took the head off a man called Del, and Marcus drove the wreck to a friend Warren's garage, where a soft-spoken fixer had them hosed down in the yard and put into borrowed shorts and T-shirts before they walked the briefcase into Otis's bar looking like schoolboys.

The warning held. Days later, over coffee, two strangers decided the diner they were sitting in hadn't been robbed lately and pulled a gun across the booth; Marcus talked the man down, handed over his own wallet, and let them walk, keeping only the briefcase, as if the miracle in the bathroom owed something forward.

Rollo, meanwhile, bought heroin from a dealer named Kip and took Nadia — Otis's wife — dancing at a diner done up like an old film, the two of them barefoot and winning the contest, Rollo never once touching her the way she'd expected. She found the bag in his coat later and took it for cocaine, went blue on Kip's carpet, and came back only for the adrenaline driven into her chest.

The watch outlasted all of it, going out of the city on Denny's wrist while the rest stayed behind, spent.

The warehouse smelled like diesel and blood, and Mr. Ash held Danny's head off the concrete like it might break if he let it fall.

"Nobody dies here today," he said. "You hear me. Nobody."

Danny heard him from somewhere far off, past the pain, past the running list of things he had told himself in a safe room a lifetime ago. Pruitt's voice, patient, going over the same lie until it wasn't a lie anymore. A bag of drugs, four dogs, a bathroom stall. Say it again. Say it until you believe it. He'd said it to Bram and Cal and Ash in a bar with a room full of men who'd heard every kind of liar there was, and they'd laughed in the right place, and that was that. He was in. They gave him a name he hadn't chosen and it stuck to him like paint.

He'd thought about that morning at the diner, eight men arguing about a pop song and whether the waitress deserved her tip, nobody using a name that was real. He'd thought about the way Bram doled out the tree names off a list, and how Birch had spent a full minute complaining that his was the worst of the lot. He'd thought about Ren walking out of prison that same week, straight into Bram's office, collecting an envelope and a seat on the crew for years of silence.

None of it mattered now. The job had come apart in under a minute — alarms already going before they were out the door, Ash firing through glass in three directions while the car fishtailed down the wrong street. Danny had gone out a side door on foot and ended up dragging a woman from her own car, and she'd had a gun in the door pocket, and now there was a hole in him leaking out everything he had left, and she was dead in the street behind him.

Birch showed up clean, timings already worked out in his head, saying the police had been on the pavement before the first alarm, saying someone in that room had made a call. He hid the stones outside where no one could watch him do it and came back in with nothing on him but fury.

Then Ren arrived, unhurried, complaining about the noise, and opened his boot and pulled out a young cop named Doyle with his wrists bound.

Left alone with him, Ren found an oldie on the radio and danced a few steps and took the man's ear off with a razor, talked into the wound, then soaked him in petrol like it was nothing at all.

That was when Danny, on the floor, put everything he had left into the gun and emptied it into Ren.

He told Doyle what he was then — a cop, he said, there are cars out there waiting for Bram — because the man deserved that much before whatever came next.

Cal walked in on the aftermath, listened to Danny's account, decided it held together, and then shot Doyle three times anyway, to close it clean.

Which was where they were now. Ash cradling him, refusing every fact in front of his face. Bram arrived and looked down at Danny for a long, flat moment.

"That's the one," Bram said. "That's our man."

Ash put his gun on Bram instead. "You don't know what you're saying."

Three guns came up in a room the size of a garage, and all three went off, and when the noise stopped only Ash and Danny were still breathing.

Danny looked up at him, at the blood on both of them, and told him — plainly, because the man had earned it — that everything Ash had refused to believe was true.

Ash's face didn't change so much as go still. He dragged himself upright, put the barrel to his own temple, and the doors came off their hinges as he pulled the trigger, and the officers pouring through cut him down where he knelt, already gone.

Martin Kray sat behind a gray desk and watched a soft-spoken man named Elias Prine fail every test put in front of him. The memory would not hold; that much was plain. But plain wasn't the same as real. Martin wrote it down as something the mind does to itself, and the insurer paid nothing, and Elias went home to a wife who would not believe her husband's mind could simply stop keeping him.

Two men came through the bathroom door that night. Martin shot one across his wife's body and the other put his head into the mirror, and from that moment nothing new would stay in him at all.

Elias's wife tested her husband the way you test a scale — asked for her injection, then asked again, wound the clock forward and asked once more. He gave her each one like it was the first, because to him it was.

Martin built himself into a filing cabinet. Photographs. Captions in block capitals. Facts cut into his own skin where no year could erode them.

She died of the dose he could not remember giving.

A plainclothes officer named Roy walked Martin through evidence a year later, out to a derelict building past the edge of town, and stood by while Martin put a bullet in the man who'd gotten out of the house that night. Within minutes Martin was asking who they were looking for.

In an insurance office, months earlier in the telling but already behind him in the living of it, Martin had closed the Prine file and moved on to the next claim, never once wondering why the name would keep surfacing in his own mouth like a coin he couldn't stop turning up.

In a motel room he didn't remember taking, Martin held the phone to his ear and told a stranger the whole Prine story again, the wife, the injections, the overdose, as if it belonged to someone else.

Martin burned a hairbrush and two paperbacks in a field, trying to grieve something he couldn't hold long enough to finish grieving.

The voice on the phone gave him a name — Gil Marsh, a dealer, an address. Martin wrote it down as fact, because a written fact was the only kind he had.

He killed Gil in a basement with water on the floor, a belt and his own hands, and then took the photograph.

Elias's wife had died believing her husband; the caller believed nothing, and asked Martin nothing, only fed him what he needed to keep moving.

Dying, Gil whispered a name — Elias — that meant nothing to Martin, who couldn't ask again. He put on the dead man's suit and drove off in the dead man's car.

Roy found him at the derelict building and told him plainly: the dealer was nobody, the revenge had already happened a year ago, and the story Martin told down telephones to strangers wasn't a case file at all. It was his own house, his own wife, his own hands.

Rather than carry that, Martin burned the photographs of Gil, wrote *he is lying to you* across Roy's picture, and copied the plate off the car outside as the next thing he would be certain of.

At a tattoo parlor he had it inked into his thigh under five other facts, not remembering the note that had brought him there.

Behind her bar, a woman named Corinne recognized the suit and the car pulling up outside, and smiled, and had the staff spit in his beer before it reached him.

She cleared every pen from her house, said the things that would make him swing, waited outside for the bruises to rise, then came back in blaming a man named Vance.

Martin took Vance apart in a motel bathroom and drove him to the edge of town at gunpoint, warning him of things he would never remember warning him of.

Corinne ran the plate through a friend at the registry and put the printout in his hand: Roy Mercer, in full.

Martin brought Roy out to the same derelict building on a pretext, walked him into the same room where a year before Roy had helped him end it once, and put a bullet through his head, and photographed what was left, certain, at last, that the note had been right all along.

A plainclothes officer named Roy walked Martin through evidence a year later, out to a derelict building past the edge of town, and stood by while Martin put a bullet in the man who'd gotten out of the house that night. Within minutes Martin was asking who they were looking for.

Martin burned a hairbrush and two paperbacks in a field, trying to grieve something he couldn't hold long enough to finish grieving.

The word rolled off Emmett Rusk's lips a second time, and then he let the globe go. It rolled off the boards and broke against the step, and no one in the room besides a nurse two doors down heard the small sound of the glass, or the word, which was Bluebell.

The screening room was full of cigarette smoke when the obituary reel ran. Nine minutes. The palace, the two papers, the two wives, the governor's race he lost by fraud he had printed himself, the collapse into that half-finished house on the hill. It explained the outside of a man completely and the inside of him not at all, and it ended on Silvermount's black windows without ever saying what Bluebell meant.

Nash was given the job because nobody else wanted it. He started with the second wife, drunk at four in the afternoon at a table in a seaside club, and she told him to get out before he finished asking.

So he went backward instead, the only direction anyone would give him anything.

He read Barrow's memoir in a marble library that still smelled of packing straw, and there it all was, the part the reel had skipped. A boarding house out west, a lodger who couldn't pay and left a worthless deed behind that turned out to sit over a seam the size of a county. A mother at a kitchen table signing her son over to a banker from the east while the father objected uselessly from the doorway. A boy in the yard driving his sled into that banker's stomach hard enough to sit him down, and being taken east that evening anyway, because a sled in a boy's hands changes nothing a grown man has already decided.

On his twenty-fifth birthday the whole estate had become his, and out of all of it — mines, rails, buildings with his name cut into their stone — he'd told Barrow he wanted the Clarion, a paper losing money every week, because he thought it might be fun. He moved a bed into the offices, put Marsh on one side of him and Devlin on the other, and printed a signed declaration of principle on the front page over his own name. Then he hired away the whole staff of the paper across the street simply by paying more, and threw them a party with a brass band and a line of dancers, and danced in the middle of it himself.

He went abroad for statuary and came home engaged to Adele, the governor's niece, and the wedding was on every front page but his own. Then came the breakfasts — longer tables, shorter talk, until they sat at either end reading rival papers, one of which he owned.

Then Nora, mud on his coat, a shopgirl laughing at him outside a chemist's, evenings at her rooms that he told no one about. Ten days before the ballot, Halloran had brought Adele up those stairs and offered him a trade — withdraw, or be ruined by Monday — and been thrown out of the building for his trouble. FRAUD AT THE POLLS ran six columns wide when he lost anyway. Devlin asked for another city. Adele left without a word from either of them.

He married Nora and bought her a voice she didn't have, a teacher, a house to sing in. The debut was unbearable. Devlin, drunk, fell asleep over half a written sentence of review, and Emmett finished it himself, in the same cruel direction, printed it, and fired him. Nora swallowed poison rather than go out before them again, and when she could speak she said so, and he finally let her stop — by shutting her away instead, in Silvermount, where she did jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station.

A black-beach picnic nobody enjoyed, a quarrel, and in the morning she packed. He wrecked her room afterward with his hands and stopped at a glass globe full of snow, said the one word to no one, and carried it past mirrors that gave him back smaller and smaller.

Marsh, Devlin, Nora again, old Colm the butler — Nash sat with all of them and got fragments, no answer. He put his notebook away, deciding no single word ever explains a life, while below him workmen cleared the last crates from the hall and fed a small child's sled, painted with one word, into the furnace.

I. THE HOUSE

Four adults, a baby and a dog in a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch, his mother kept the peace, and he spent most of his days watching his brother's wife move through the kitchen like something he had no right to want.

Nestor robbed a chemist's at night with a scarf over his face and came home to knock Alma across the room for asking where the money had gone. Ruben started saying, quietly and then not quietly, that she should come away with him.

He noticed what the dog was worth around the same time. Tigre came back from the street having killed something bigger than itself, and a neighbour explained the arithmetic. Within a month the dog was going into the pit twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben understood there was enough in it to leave on.

So he paid two men in a bar to give his brother an address, and gave them Nestor's. Nestor came out of hospital, worked out who'd arranged it inside a day, and left with the wife, the baby, and every note hidden in the wardrobe.

The promoter shot the dog in the ring when a fight went against him, and Ruben went over the rope with a knife and was in the truck with Pipo before anyone moved, the dog bleeding across the back seat.

Nestor went into a bank with the same scarf, months later, and was shot on the floor of it. At the funeral Ruben made his offer to Alma one last time. She looked at him and said no, and meant it, and he understood then that she had never once meant yes.

II. THE FLAT

A married man walked out on a wife and two daughters at a birthday party and moved a model named Celine into a flat with a wall of glass facing her own image on the hoarding across the street.

She woke in hospital with steel pins holding her leg together and asked first about the lapdog, which had been alone in the new flat and had not been seen since.

Chispa had gone through a gap in the floorboards and could not get out, and her whining came up through every room. Hector tore the boards up one by one with a crowbar while Celine's leg went bad above him.

It came off above the knee in the end. That same week the hoarding was stripped and pasted over with something else, and the two of them sat in the wrecked flat looking at a blank frame where she used to be.

III. THE JUNCTION AND AFTER

The truck came through a red light at sixty and took the side out of a small car turning across the junction — Celine's car.

A vagrant pushing a scrap cart stood in the smoke, looked at both wrecks and the people running toward them, and lifted the bleeding dog out of the back seat and walked away with it. His name was Cardo.

He nursed the dog back to health over weeks in a yard full of strays, feeding it by hand, and it slept against him and followed him out each morning.

A man in a good suit met Cardo behind a church, handed him a photograph of his own half-brother and business partner, and named a price. Cardo took half in advance and asked nothing.

He stood far back at his own wife's burial, among people who believed him twenty years dead, then followed his grown daughter through three streets and stopped outside her building.

Tigre killed every other dog in the yard while Cardo was out. He came home to the bodies and one dog standing wet-muzzled among them, put the gun to its head, held it there, and sat down on the ground unable to fire.

He took Sergio off a pavement without difficulty and, instead of killing him, chained him to a bed frame among the empty kennels. Later he brought Elian to sit across from the brother he'd paid to have killed, laid a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked out with money from both.

He let himself into Perla's flat while she was at work, sat on her bed an hour, and left a long message on the machine — who he was, where he'd gone, why — and took one photograph off the shelf.

Shaved, in clothes that didn't fit him, he left the money on her table, took the dog, and walked out across the flat grey ground at the edge of the city, with nothing between him and the horizon but the animal at his heel.

Nadir stood at the counter with Sahar beside him, translating the things he already understood, while the man behind the glass repeated his vowels back at him in a mocking singsong for the benefit of nobody. Nadir paid for the gun and left with his daughter, humiliated, armed, and certain he had done something necessary.

He did not know yet that months later he would stand outside a house at dusk with that same pistol in his coat, waiting for a locksmith to come out his own front door.

Two young men walked up a restaurant pavement, laughing about who was watching them, and then they weren't laughing, they had pistols out and a prosecutor's car keys in Trey's hand while Halstead's wife Paula screamed on the kerb. Later the same wife would stand at the top of her stairs and tell her husband, loud enough for the locksmith fitting their new locks to hear every word, that the tattooed one would sell their keys to his friends by morning. Mateo said nothing and finished the job.

A patrol car pulled the Hobarts over for no reason at all. Boyle had them out on the hood, and his hand went where it had no business going while Clay stood three feet away and said nothing. His partner Voss watched from beside the car and, the next morning, went to their commander and said he couldn't ride with the man anymore. He got his new car by claiming Boyle had a flatulence problem, and told himself that settled it.

Mateo fitted a new lock into Nadir's door and said the lock wasn't the issue, the door itself needed replacing. Nadir heard a man inventing a second job for himself and threw him out.

It was that refusal that would matter later, when the door came off its hinges in the night and the insurer read the file and declined to pay a cent, citing the warning Nadir himself had refused.

Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank, begging for a referral for his dying father, and when she said no he came apart at her name badge like it was her fault the world worked this way.

Some time after that — though the man crawling into the wreck to drag Renee out through a gap in a burning car did not know it would ever come back around this way — it was Boyle's hands on her belt, Boyle's arms around her, the same hands from the roadside, hauling her clear before the fire reached the tank.

Trey and Kwame, driving Halstead's stolen car, caught a small man named Pham crossing between vans and left him folded and breathing outside a hospital door, arguing the whole way there about whose fault it was.

Clay was pulled from his own car at gunpoint by four officers who'd been told it was stolen, and Voss walked into the middle of it and talked them down. Clay drove away afterward with Trey crouched in his passenger seat, and three miles out he stopped the car and put the boy out on the verge in the dark without a word — the boy who had tried to rob him.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house that evening with the gun in his coat. Mateo came out the door and Nadir raised it, shouting, and Rosie ran off the porch into her father's arms just as it fired. Nothing happened. No one was hit. It came out afterward that Sahar, sent to buy ammunition, had quietly bought the box that did nothing at all, and Nadir decided the child was his angel.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain, saw a hand go for a pocket, and put two rounds into Kwame before burning the car. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the ditch, walked over with his hands in his pockets, and stopped, because he knew the shoes. His mother, on her kitchen floor, told him she'd asked him a hundred times to go and look for his brother and he never once went.

Paula fell down her own stairs and lay there until Alba found her, and in the ambulance said she was the only friend she had.

Trey bought Pham's wrecked van cheap, opened the back expecting stock, and found two dozen people paid for in the dark. He drove them to the docks and let them go.

The first snow came that winter, and two cars touched at a junction, and the shouting started before either driver had looked at the damage.

Above the noise, at an open window, the old man was still talking. "Nothing survives," he said. "Not the good nights, not the bad ones. Time takes them the same way." The younger man beside him said nothing, only watched the street below, where blue light was sliding over brick and glass, and two men were being carried out through a crowd with their hands behind them, one shouting, one silent.

They had been arrested for what had happened minutes before in the basement below the pavement — for the man Jonah had gone on hitting with a fire extinguisher long after he'd stopped moving, while a few feet away, watching with everyone else, the man they had actually come for stood and did nothing to stop it.

They had come to that club because two men in a doorway had offered, for money, to sell them a name and had pointed the way down the street. They had wanted the name because they had come out of a party laughing and stopped laughing at the sight of a trolley and a blanket and a face they both knew.

She had been on that trolley because she had walked into a tiled underpass to avoid four lanes of headlights and found a man they called the Adder holding a woman by the hair, explaining something to her with his fist, and when he was finished with the woman he had turned, unhurried, and started on her instead, going on hitting her head against the concrete while a passer-by at the far end of the tunnel looked, hesitated, and left.

She had taken the underpass because she had left the party alone, coat over her arm, having watched Cort drink past the point of being any fun and start working the room for someone else, and having decided, without a word to anyone, that she was not staying to watch the rest of it.

They had gone to the party at all riding the underground together, the three of them swaying in the carriage, arguing cheerfully about sex and about how much Cort had already had to drink, the kind of argument people have when they expect to have it again tomorrow.

Before that there had been an afternoon in a park, sprinklers turning over cut grass, children running through the spray, and Lise lying on her side with a book she wasn't really reading, one hand resting flat on her stomach, in a day that had begun in complete safety.

Before that, alone in the flat, she had sat on the edge of the bath with the stick in both hands and let herself smile at it before telling anyone at all.

And before that, in the grey light of morning, she had lain in bed with Cort telling him about a dream — a red tunnel she kept walking into, over and over, and the two of them had traded lazy insults about Jonah, who used to live with her and was only a friend now, easy the way people are easy when nothing has happened to them yet.

"You'll notice," the old man said, "that I'm not complaining. It isn't a complaint. It's only what's true." The younger man turned from the window at last. "What was destroyed, exactly?" he asked, and the old man looked down at the street, at the lights receding now, at the ordinary dark folding back over the doorway and the pavement and the tiled mouth of the underpass two streets away, and did not answer straightaway.

"A morning," he said finally. "An afternoon in a park. A woman who hadn't told anyone yet. Two men who thought they loved her enough to fix it." He shrugged, the way a man shrugs at weather. "None of it left a mark you could point to twenty years from now. That's the whole of what I'm telling you. Not that it didn't matter. That it didn't survive."

Below, the last of the crowd was dispersing, and somewhere under the road a woman none of them would ever thank was still lying on tile that had not yet been cleaned, and the city went on arranging itself around the absence of all of them, patient, indifferent, already forgetting the shape of the night.

I did not sleep for six months. Then I found the trick: a church hall, folding chairs, a dying stranger's arms around my shoulders while I sobbed about grief that wasn't mine, and I would go home and sleep like something switched off. Four evenings a week, I sat in those rooms and wept for diseases I did not have.

Then a woman started coming. Ada. She smoked through the meditation and made no effort to hide that she was faking, and the moment I saw the lie in her I saw it in myself, and the sleep stopped again.

On a flight not long after, I sat beside a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, who talked for forty minutes about how nothing either of us owned had been chosen by us. I put his card in my pocket and forgot him, or thought I had.

I want to tell you now about the window. Later — much later than anything I've told you yet — Ada was brought to me by shaven men who apologized and left, and we stood at a high window with my face wrapped in gauze, holding hands, watching towers go down one after another in careful order, like something obeying its own schedule. I didn't understand that scene when it happened to me the first time. I only understood it once I'd lived all the way up to it.

But before that: my flat exploded. I came home to my windows on the pavement and everything in it gone, and I called the salesman instead of the woman I should have called, and he took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and no reason I should have trusted him.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park and I had never felt anything so clearly. It became a weekly thing in a cellar, rules read aloud, a waiting list of men wanting to be hit by strangers.

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the house, and the two of them were audible through every floor while I lay rigid below them, unable to say why it undid me the way it did.

Rex started boiling stolen fat from a cosmetic clinic into soap on the kitchen stove, selling it back to the stores at eighty dollars a bar. He held my hand flat on the table and poured lye across it and would not let me leave my body to escape the burn. He made me stay in the minute.

I walked into my employer's office and beat my own face into the carpet until security found us, and after that I was paid to stay away.

The cellar became an organization. Rex called it Havoc. The house filled with shaved recruits who slept on floors and went out to vandalize corporate property in his name, and I could not say when it had stopped being mine.

Rex drove us into oncoming traffic on a wet road, let the car roll, and when I came round in the ditch he was gone and stayed gone.

Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to shut the whole thing down.

I flew from city to city and found the same cellar under every bar, the same rules on the same walls, and strangers who looked up and called me Rex Marrow.

In a motel room, with flight records and receipts spread over the bed, it went together: one body, one bank account, one man, awake and asleep. There had never been a second man. I called Ada and asked, badly, whose bed she'd been in. His, she said, obviously — yours — and asked what was wrong with me.

Then I found the charges wired into the towers that held every debt record in the city, and understood what all of it had been for.

Rex beat me down a stairwell, and at the bottom I understood the gun in his hand was in my own. I put it in my mouth and fired through my cheek to kill him.

And that is how I come to be standing at the window with Ada, holding hands, watching the buildings fall in their patient, arranged order.

The helicopters came over at night, low and steady, laying poison for the fruit fly across every roof in the city, and nobody who heard them slept quite the same after.

Under that same drone, Neil buttoned a fresh shirt for the second time while Bess worked on a canvas of unfinished bodies until the last possible minute, neither of them saying much about who was coming to dinner. Across town Cheryl folded nappies with the phone against her ear, telling a stranger things she wasn't doing, while Stu sat three feet away going quietly incandescent. In a jazz club with low light, Vida sang the standards beautifully to people who mostly talked through them, and at home her daughter Bee practiced cello alone in a house that never quite had two people in the same room. On the far side of the valley, Officer Rowe put the family dog out of the car and drove home to tell Peg it must have jumped the fence — a lie built for Nan, who did not yet know that her ex-husband Cass had heard she had a new man.

Elaine had already been to the bakery that week, choosing a design from Otto's book and writing a boy's name and age on a card. Charlie was seven the following Monday. On his way to school he stepped off the kerb and a waitress named Rhona, hurrying, caught him with the wing of her car. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home insisting on it.

He seemed fine until the evening he wasn't. He went to sleep on the sofa and didn't wake up properly, and after that there was a hospital room, a machine, and Grant and Elaine trading the chair between them. Duff turned up in the corridor with a coffee and, having nothing better to offer the silence, told his estranged son about a woman he'd known decades ago. Grant said nothing back.

Nobody had collected the cake. Nobody had paid for it. Otto, unpaid and unable to bear being ignored, began ringing the house at two in the morning to say the boy's name into the receiver.

Cass, having learned about Nan's new man, spent an afternoon sawing her chairs, her table, her bedframe into pieces. Meanwhile Stu and three friends, including Vern, walked two hours upriver to fish and found a young woman face down in the shallows. They tied a line around her ankle so she wouldn't drift, and kept fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern finally told it the way it got told at the pub, his wife Iris stopped wiping off her clown makeup halfway through, sponge in hand, disgusted at what he'd been willing to stand beside.

At the Hartigans', house-sitters Ike and Dot made each other up as a beaten corpse and photographed it in the hall, laughing, while Neil and Bess's dinner party ran its course above them — until Bess admitted, over the fish, the modelling session and the affair after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene.

The machine was switched off the next morning. Charlie died, and that afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at Otto about the calls. Instead he sat them down, fed them warm bread, and wept with them — learning, too late, whose birthday the cake had been for.

Bee came home from rehearsal to find her mother asleep in the chair as always. She closed the garage door and left the engine running.

At a picnic in the hills, a girl said the wrong ordinary thing, and Stu, who had been carrying something since the river, picked up a rock.

That evening the ground shook for eleven seconds. By the late bulletin, the tremor, the wrecks, Charlie, Bee, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills — all of it folded into the same three minutes of news, and the city went on to weather in the morning.

Solly Two Coats and his crew walked into the diamond house dressed as pilgrims, heads bowed, hands folded, and walked out with a stone the size of a knuckle. By the time they'd shed the robes in a rented room, Marv was already on the phone from overseas, voice thin and hard down the wire: bring it straight over, no detours, no cleverness.

Grigor the Nail did two things with the same breath. He told Solly about a bookmaker's shop where a man could get a fair price laid on a fixed fight, and he told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno about a bookmaker's shop worth robbing. He didn't mention it was the same shop.

Across the city, the promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan off the travellers. Sam said something he shouldn't have to a bare-knuckle brawler named Finn, and went down in the dirt before he could finish the sentence. That left Halloway without a fighter for Coldstone's rigged bout, and only one man standing who could hit like that. He promised Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round. Coldstone believed him because Halloway had no choice but to be believed.

Solly landed in the city that same week, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty-looking case to the bookmaker's to place his bet. Ike, Benno and a third man, Tulley, botched the robbery entirely, tearing the case from Solly's arm along with the arm itself in the scramble, then fleeing when Grigor arrived to see what his tip had produced.

Finn, in his fixed bout, forgot the fourth round entirely and put his man down in the first. Coldstone lost a fortune and put his hands on Halloway's collar to explain what that meant.

Marv flew in behind schedule, found no cousin and no stone, and hired a bounty hunter named Ledge, a man who found things by following the men too stupid to hide them well.

Grigor took Solly apart to open the case and found nothing inside but air where a diamond should have been.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces on a quiet street, and took Ike, Benno, and the stone they'd since recovered.

Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby, calmly, what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway told Finn again: fourth round. That night Coldstone's men burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan, to make certain the message held.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with the pawnbrokers inside. In the gunfire Ledge died, Grigor died, and Benno died with them, three claims on the diamond erased in a single street.

Tulley walked away from the wreckage with nothing but a dog — the same dog that had swallowed the stone days earlier without anyone noticing.

Finn waited, this time, until the fourth round exactly, and then knocked his man out cold, while the travellers he'd grown up among moved quietly through the crowd and put an end to Coldstone's men one by one, camp debt for camp debt.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone after the massacre and shot him where he stood. By morning the travellers had folded their camp and vanished, leaving no one to answer for it.

The dog turned up weeks later, handed in at a pet shop by someone who didn't want it anymore, and coughed up a diamond onto the counter in front of the astonished owner. Word reached Halloway and Digby before anyone else thought to claim it, and so the two promoters, who had never robbed anything in their lives, ended up holding the stone that had cost so many people theirs.

Listen: he says he has come unstuck in time, and that is the only way to tell it, because there is no other way that is honest.

He is on a lecture platform, addressing a crowd about the moment of his own death, which he has always known, and then he is being shot by a beam weapon exactly as he foresaw, and the crowd does not understand that this was not a surprise to him at all.

He is a boy in a small industrial town, weak and peculiar, the kind of child who does not fit the shape his father wants him to fit.

He is at the bottom of a swimming pool, having been thrown there by that same father to teach him to swim, and he finds that the bottom is not an unpleasant place, that he does not feel any urgency to leave it.

He is married to the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school, and he is rich, and none of it seems to have cost him anything, though of course it did.

He is in the mountains, in the wreckage of an airplane, alive, while his wife is dying of exhaust fumes on the road to the hospital where he is being kept, and these two facts sit next to each other without touching.

He is in a radio studio telling the world about a planet where he was kept in a zoo with a film actress, and about aliens who explained to him that every moment that ever was or will be is happening all the time, and that free will is a notion peculiar only to Earth.

He is behind enemy lines with a scout who beats him because he wants to be left where he has fallen, the way he once wanted to be left at the bottom of the pool.

He is on a prison train, and the scout is dying of gangrene beside him, and with his last breath the scout blames him for it, and this blame travels forward through the war and past it like a thing with its own momentum, though no one watching him now would know that yet.

He is in a camp beside enemy officers who have, through some clerical error, been drawing double rations for years, fat in their uniforms while the new prisoners arrive starved, and he thinks this is very funny in the way that nothing is funny.

He is his daughter's problem, being told he is senile, having his affairs taken out of his hands, because she has heard him on the radio talking about the fourth dimension and cannot think what else it could mean.

He is in a city that is destroyed by fire in a single night while he sleeps below it in a disused abattoir with the other prisoners, and in the morning they come up the stairs into a place that used to be a city and no longer is.

He is digging bodies out of a cellar with the others until one of them dies of the dry heaves, doing this over and over, and there is no way to say how many days this takes because the days have stopped mattering.

He is in a hospital after the war, collapsed, and another patient hands him some books by a hack writer of science fiction, paperbacks with lurid covers, and something in them fits him the way nothing else has.

He is in a transparent room on another planet with a film actress, and the aliens outside the glass are explaining to him, patiently, the way you would explain something to a child, that there is no such thing as now.

He is a chaplain's assistant shipped overseas with no training worth the name, carrying a Bible he does not know what to do with.

He is being told, by a fellow prisoner who has taken up the dead scout's grievance as his own, that one day, no matter how many years pass, he will be killed for it.

And he is on the platform again, the beam weapon flashing, the crowd gasping, and he is not surprised, having always known this was where he would arrive, if arrival is even the word for a place you have already been.

Emlyn arrived at Wilder's house that same evening, still in the coat he'd worn to his own office, and sat down across from the man who had telephoned him in a state he could not name over the wire.

"You've spoken to Odile," Emlyn said, before Wilder could arrange his face into any particular shape.

"She told me everything last night. She says she told you."

"She told me on the boat," Emlyn said. "Four years ago. There was a letter waiting for her at the hotel desk, in a hand I knew as well as my own — better, probably, than I know most things about you. I asked her about it over drinks. She didn't lie particularly well." He looked at the room, at the bottles Wilder kept for guests he no longer entertained. "I read your letters too, some of them. I never thought much of your prose style, if I'm honest. Too many qualifications. You write like a man asking permission."

Wilder said nothing, because there was nothing that would not sound absurd.

Two years before that evening, in a bar that smelled of wet coats, Odile had told him her marriage was over, that she'd spent the previous night confessing to Emlyn as though the confession were new, a gift or a wound she was only now delivering. She had mentioned, almost as an afterthought, stirring her glass, that Emlyn had lately been publishing some writer Wilder represented and despised — a small, ordinary betrayal of taste that seemed, in the moment, larger than the marriage itself. Wilder had gone home unable to eat, and it was that detail, more than the confession, which had driven him to the telephone.

Before that, though — long before, in the calendar the story insists on running backward from — there had been the closing of the rooms. Wilder and Odile had stood among divided crockery, deciding without ceremony that the flat in the quiet district had become a chore rather than a refuge, and they had surrendered the lease with the mild relief of people cancelling a subscription. No one had been caught. The affair had simply grown tired of its own furniture.

Earlier than that, dinner at Emlyn and Odile's house, where the two men talked racquets and old schoolboy scores until Odile might as well have been the maid clearing the plates. Earlier still, a long restaurant lunch in which Emlyn baited Wilder about contemporary fiction with a viciousness that seemed literary and was not, while never once naming the thing he already knew.

Before the lunch: the hotel, the letter, the confession, and Emlyn's strange calm — his admission that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife, said the way a man might admit to a mild lifelong illness. Odile had gone home from that trip and said nothing whatever to Wilder about it; the rented rooms received her exactly as before, and the afternoon passed like all the others, false in a way that felt, at the time, like fidelity.

Before that: Odile announcing she was carrying her husband's child, and the two of them deciding, in the manner of people rearranging furniture rather than lives, that the rooms would go on unaltered.

Before that: the rooms themselves, filled with linen and plates as though ordinary objects could domesticate what they were doing, could make of the affair a second marriage with better manners.

Emlyn arrived at Wilder's house that same evening, still in the coat he'd worn to his own office, and sat down across from the man who had telephoned him in a state he could not name over the wire.

"You've spoken to Odile," Emlyn said, before Wilder could arrange his face into any particular shape.

"She told me everything last night. She says she told you."

"She told me on the boat," Emlyn said. "Four years ago. There was a letter waiting for her at the hotel desk, in a hand I knew as well as my own — better, probably, than I know most things about you. I asked her about it over drinks. She didn't lie particularly well." He looked at the room, at the bottles Wilder kept for guests he no longer entertained. "I read your letters too, some of them. I never thought much of your prose style, if I'm honest. Too many qualifications. You write like a man asking permission."

Wilder said nothing, because there was nothing that would not sound absurd.

Two years before that evening, in a bar that smelled of wet coats, Odile had told him her marriage was over, that she'd spent the previous night confessing to Emlyn as though the confession were new, a gift or a wound she was only now delivering. She had mentioned, almost as an afterthought, stirring her glass, that Emlyn had lately been publishing some writer Wilder represented and despised — a small, ordinary betrayal of taste that seemed, in the moment, larger than the marriage itself. Wilder had gone home unable to eat, and it was that detail, more than the confession, which had driven him to the telephone.

Before that, though — long before, in the calendar the story insists on running backward from — there had been the closing of the rooms. Wilder and Odile had stood among divided crockery, deciding without ceremony that the flat in the quiet district had become a chore rather than a refuge, and they had surrendered the lease with the mild relief of people cancelling a subscription. No one had been caught. The affair had simply grown tired of its own furniture.

Earlier than that, dinner at Emlyn and Odile's house, where the two men talked racquets and old schoolboy scores until Odile might as well have been the maid clearing the plates. Earlier still, a long restaurant lunch in which Emlyn baited Wilder about contemporary fiction with a viciousness that seemed literary and was not, while never once naming the thing he already knew.

Before the lunch: the hotel, the letter, the confession, and Emlyn's strange calm — his admission that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife, said the way a man might admit to a mild lifelong illness. Odile had gone home from that trip and said nothing whatever to Wilder about it; the rented rooms received her exactly as before, and the afternoon passed like all the others, false in a way that felt, at the time, like fidelity.

Before that: Odile announcing she was carrying her husband's child, and the two of them deciding, in the manner of people rearranging furniture rather than lives, that the rooms would go on unaltered.

Before that: the rooms themselves, filled with linen and plates as though ordinary objects could domesticate what they were doing, could make of the affair a second marriage with better manners.

And before all of it, the party at Emlyn's house, the noise of other people's voices rising through the floor, Wilder leading Odile up the stairs and telling her, in the small room above all that celebration, how lovely she was — the words which had seemed, at the time, like a beginning, and which now, in Wilder's house with Emlyn sitting across from him admitting he'd known for years, seemed instead like the last honest thing either of them had said.
